title: Reduced effective resolution from averaging attention-weighted positions
description: The Transformer's constant number of operations to relate signals from arbitrary positions comes at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, which the authors counteract with Multi-Head Attention.

paper.title: Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models
paper.abstract: Recent work on Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) has revealed striking limits in their working memory capacity, similar to what has been found in human behavioral studies. Specifically, these models' performance drops significantly on N-back tasks as N increases. However, there is still a lack of mechanistic interpretability as to why this phenomenon would arise. Inspired by the executive attention theory from behavioral sciences, we hypothesize that the self-attention mechanism within Transformer-based models might be responsible for their working memory capacity limits. To test this hypothesis, we train vanilla decoder-only transformers to perform N-back tasks and find that attention scores gradually aggregate to the N-back positions over training, suggesting that the model masters the task by learning a strategy to pay attention to the relationship between the current position and the N-back position. Critically, we find that the total entropy of the attention score matrix increases as N increases, suggesting that the dispersion of attention scores might be the cause of the capacity limit observed in N-back tasks. Our findings thus offer insights into the shared role of attention in both human and artificial intelligence. Moreover, the limitations of the self-attention mechanism revealed in the current study could inform future efforts to design more powerful model architectures with enhanced working memory capacity and cognitive capabilities.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper studies working memory capacity limits in Transformer-based models using N-back tasks. It shows that as N increases, attention scores become more dispersed (higher entropy), leading to decreased accuracy. The model learns to attend to the N-back position but struggles to maintain focused attention as the distance grows. The paper provides mechanistic interpretability for why Transformers perform worse on higher N-back tasks.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the gap about reduced effective resolution from averaging attention-weighted positions. That gap concerns a fundamental property of the attention mechanism: averaging weighted position representations inherently loses fine-grained positional information, which is why the original Transformer paper introduced Multi-Head Attention to counteract this loss. This paper instead studies a different phenomenon — the dispersion/spread of attention scores across positions as a function of task difficulty (N-back distance). It does not analyze or discuss the resolution loss from averaging attention-weighted positions, nor does it evaluate whether multi-head attention mitigates this issue. The gap remains entirely unaddressed.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: The gap is analytically tractable: it asks whether multi-head attention counteracts the resolution loss from averaging attention weights. No special data collection is needed — standard Transformer checkpoints (or even small toy models) suffice, and analysis can be purely mathematical or involve small-scale probing. Compute requirements are minimal (probing attention heads, measuring effective rank or entropy). The main challenge is defining "effective resolution" precisely, but multiple candidates exist (attention entropy, rank of attention matrices, mutual information between positions). Progress is clearly measurable: compare single-head vs. multi-head attention on such a metric. The scope is focused and does not require a fundamental breakthrough — it extends known analysis methods from the attention interpretability and information theory literature.
